/uk-news/2026/sep/24/police-arrest-far-r.headline: Police invoke maritime safety laws to arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas over slashed Channel dinghy
/uk-news/2026/sep/24/police-arrest-far-r.bodyHtml:
Police have arrested Daniel Thomas, the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist, on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, acting two days after he filmed himself slashing the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was on board.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said officers had arrested a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, on Wednesday night “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety under section 11 of the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990”.

Thomas was also suspected, the police said, of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals under section 58 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995”.

Thomas appears to have filmed himself being arrested on Wednesday night, and a video showing the arrest, apparently at a garage, was uploaded on to his YouTube platform. In it, an officer told him he had been “involved in criminal damage that has recklessly endangered someone’s life”.

“I understand. I knew this was coming,” said Thomas, who prefers to go by the name Danny Tommo.

Over this summer Thomas has brought dozens of nationalist protest groups together under the umbrella movement Patriot Platform.

He was behind anti-immigration marches by masked men in Dover and Portsmouth this month.

More details soon …

/politics/2026/sep/24/tactical-voting-uk.headline: Voters open to tactical voting could reshape next election, poll finds, with Reform pushed to fourth
/politics/2026/sep/24/tactical-voting-uk.bodyHtml:
Voters willing to switch to the best-placed candidate in their seat could reshape the next election, a major poll has found: if tactical voting is widespread, progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority.

The results suggest Andy Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage.

The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically. It also shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters, while the right remains split.

Such an approach would be a marked contrast to the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party tried to attract more conservative older voters, and it would be likely to unsettle some in Labour, given the same strategy was deployed for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.

The poll, which comes on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool, shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour and will encourage those in the party who are thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Since April, twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right.

Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees conducted the previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.

If an election took place today, it suggests, Labour would be the largest party in parliament on 272 seats, a four-point lead – 42% of parliamentary seats with 28% of the vote.

Reform would become the official opposition on 153 seats, 24% of the total and the same as its vote share, with the Conservatives falling to third place on 85.

Two hundred seats are tight marginals decided by under five points, so a two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats that are likely to decide a future election. And in those seats a far higher percentage of voters are open to tactical voting when they cite their preferred party – a sign of how volatile the polls remain.

Were voters prepared to switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats, rather than their preferred party, Reform UK’s seat count would fall dramatically, favouring Labour and the Conservatives.

About 18% of voters who live in a seat where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to do so but are not yet doing so. Were those voters to vote tactically, Labour would reach 319 seats – six short of a majority – and Reform UK would be reduced to 62.

Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour, though the projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.

In 59 seats, Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points. Among these are the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – all of which have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives under a scenario with more tactical voting.

In Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, which the now-chancellor, John Healey, held in 2024 with 49% of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6%, the base modelling of the MRP indicates that Reform could win a tight race, with a 51% chance, but that this plummets if tactical voting increases, with a 76% chance of Labour holding the seat in this scenario.

In Bassetlaw, tactical voting would lift Labour from 32% to 40%, meaning Reform could lose even as its own vote share rises from 35% to 40%. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place. The forecast estimates that the winner would shift from Reform, with a 77% chance, to Labour, with a 58% chance.

Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios, and under heavier tactical voting the chance of a Conservative win increases from 68% to more than 99% should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.

Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.

“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.

“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”

The sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives, where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year, also complicates the prediction. Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to opt to vote for the Conservatives, even if they were technically the best placed to beat Reform at the next election, showing the limitations of predictions around tactical voting.

Labour is also gaining considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, the poll suggests, but not from Reform. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60% to 46%; on the right, of those lost to Reform or the Tories, it has fallen from 27% to 24%.

Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling indicated a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, while also showing significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.

“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”

/education/2026/sep/24/indian-oil-gas-he.headline: Newcastle University sets out its case for Anant Ambani sustainability professorship as conservationists question it
/education/2026/sep/24/indian-oil-gas-he.bodyHtml:
Newcastle University has set out its reasons for appointing the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune, who runs a controversial mega-zoo, as a professor of sustainability, as it faces a backlash from conservationists over the decision.

Anant Ambani has been given a professorship of practice, the university announced, for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare, and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.

Ambani is the son of Mukesh Ambani, India’s richest person, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations, and the prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.

Anant Ambani, who is 31, leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn. He has also set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.

Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing, although conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species.

Academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists responded to the announcement with incredulity and derision.

Ramachandra Guha, the author of Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism and a leading Indian public intellectual, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts, etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.

“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”

Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator of the illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”

Prof Matt Perry, the chair of Newcastle University’s University and College Union branch, said staff members had raised objections to the appointment, citing environmental concerns.

Prof Lyla Mehta, who heads the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.

She added: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”

Anant Ambani launched Vantara University in April, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.

Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”

An investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung in 2025 found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.

India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing in August last year after an investigation that lasted less than three weeks. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were likely forged.

“There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals,” the report found. Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals, but subsequently reversed its decision after India, the US and Japan objected at a Cites meeting, arguing there was not enough proof of illegal imports.

The zoo launched a “reset” of its operations in August, appointing a former Cites head to oversee them, and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.

The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking, saying: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.” Vantara has declined to comment.

A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

/us-news/2026/sep/24/judge-orders-trump-.headline: Judge orders press passes returned to CNN, MS Now and Politico, saying Trump ban likely unconstitutional
/us-news/2026/sep/24/judge-orders-trump-.bodyHtml:
A federal judge has ordered the administration to temporarily restore White House access to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, saying Trump’s ban on the three media outlets was likely unconstitutional.

US district judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organizations filed contesting the ban, which the president announced on 18 September.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to return the outlets’ press passes immediately, issuing a temporary restraining order that will be in effect for 14 days. Such orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo while the court gives the case a closer review.

Earlier on Wednesday Kelly had set out the past case law that clearly established the need for a distinct process, one involving advance notice of an infraction and the opportunity to plead one’s case.

Prior cases made clear, the judge said, “before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard”.

The judge signalled skepticism when a Justice Department lawyer told him the Trump administration had provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the press passes in letters sent to the news outlets on Tuesday, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed.

Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” and justice department lawyers had sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, arguing that the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They asked for a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out.

The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president has the authority to suspend access by news organizations.

The three outlets also have the support of a coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organizations, which filed a legal brief on Wednesday backing them and asserting that “stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of supreme court jurisprudence.”

Signatories to the brief included the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.

With Reuters and the Associated Press

/world/2026/sep/24/netanyahu-to-deliver-.headline: Netanyahu to ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ in UN speech as protests and a walkout are planned
/world/2026/sep/24/netanyahu-to-deliver-.bodyHtml:
Benjamin Netanyahu will take the stage at the UN on Thursday to deliver a familiar message of defiance, in a speech his ambassador says will set out ‘what still should be done’ – even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation.

The speech comes as Netanyahu faces the toughest re-election challenge of a political career spanning decades, with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

Internationally, the UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, part of growing condemnation of Israel, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.

In the US, public opinion is in the midst of a historic shift against Israel: 62% of respondents told Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hope he is voted out in October.

New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, assured demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”, tempering his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal, as protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the city’s streets.

Speaking in a telephone interview before this week’s speech, Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, defended Netanyahu’s government and sought to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.

“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” Danon said. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”

He added: “At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us.”

Organisers have scheduled several protests in New York City on Thursday, where anger at Netanyahu will be on full display, including one from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.

Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said: “Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here.”

She described a “mainstreaming” of the public view that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”

Palestinian representatives, meanwhile, are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, Danon said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?” In Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling.

The White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, though Danon did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech.

The hardline message Netanyahu is expected to deliver is aimed not just at world leaders but also at his own electorate in Israel ahead of the October elections. Miller said: “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation. And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”

The visit is expected to last less than 24 hours, and Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with Netanyahu during it. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, while Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech.

Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit, a Trump administration official said, but none was organised. Nor are there plans to meet congressional leaders, Danon said.

Top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading Democratic presidential contenders have both voiced criticism, meaning Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past.

Miller noted fractures even within the Maga base, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.

Of a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship, Danon said: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”

There are now multiple flashpoints for anger from both US political parties and from the international community, however, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.

Danon pointed to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace when asked whether a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza, saying Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”. If that does not change, he said, Israel “will do it ourselves”, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”

On the West Bank he was equally resolute, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Senate Democrats are also introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement. Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.

The protests began before Netanyahu had even arrived in New York.

Several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied on Wednesday at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport, protesting at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft.

Among the speakers was Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state. She later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting against Netanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.

“Thousands of people are against his presence in our city,” she said.

Some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, but “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.

/technology/2026/sep/24/nick-clegg-plays.headline: Nick Clegg makes the case for a calmer AI debate: transparency and ‘tramlines’, not extinction talk
/technology/2026/sep/24/nick-clegg-plays.bodyHtml:
Nick Clegg has urged tech bosses to concentrate on the specific, known risks of AI rather than its “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, dismissing such fears as a sign that they are “breathing their own fumes”.

Cybersecurity and bioweapons are the known, specific threats that tech bosses should be addressing, the former UK deputy prime minister said, rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.

He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”

Clegg said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry. He was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta, owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs.

He noted that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”. “They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said.

He said: “There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things.”

Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency” when asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face.

He said, however, that this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI, and he suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.

There was, he added, room for others to work together: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”

Clegg urged realism when asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, noting the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”

Clegg also set out why he disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence.

What he proposed instead was openness: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”

/film/2026/sep/24/global-release-announc.headline: Gaza documentary NAZA sets out cinema release in 56 territories after record Venice ovation
/film/2026/sep/24/global-release-announc.bodyHtml:
Cinemas in more than 50 countries will show NAZA, the award-winning documentary from Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, before the film has a digital global release on theguardian.com.

The Guardian-produced film premiered at the Venice film festival earlier this month, where a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record – greeted it, and the documentary went on to win the special jury prize.

Its North American premiere comes on Saturday at the New York film festival, following screenings in Bologna and at the San Sebastián film festival, and the film opens four days later at the IFC Center in New York City. Los Angeles and other key US cities follow on 9 October, ahead of a national rollout.

MK2 Films is partnering on a theatrical release planned in 55 other territories, including the UK, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Canada, Hong Kong, Brazil, Turkey, Thailand, France, Spain, Germany, Turkey, Central America and the Middle East.

Once its cinema run is complete, the Guardian will stream the film on its website, for free, as part of the news organisation’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.

“NAZA is grounded in rigorous journalism published over the past three years,” said Harry Davies, a Guardian investigations correspondent and one of NAZA’s producers. “But it is also a powerful piece of cinema that will soon be available on screens, large and small, around the world.”

The Guardian is exploring ways by which NAZA can be seen in the occupied Palestinian territories, and a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel have been offered the film.

The documentary reveals the systems behind Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. NAZA is a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike.

The film features interviews with 24 members of Israeli intelligence and military, granted on the condition of anonymity and shot at night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv. It builds on journalism first published by the Guardian, +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication, and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025.

Abraham and Szor won the best documentary Oscar in 2024 for No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning film-maker of The Zone of Interest and Under the Skin, is executive producer, and his longtime collaborator, James Wilson of JW Films, also produced the film.

Reviews at the premiere were unanimously positive, but last week Benjamin Netanyahu and a number of senior military and far-right political figures called for the directors’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of “treason against the state”.

The Israeli prime minister said he would seek new laws allowing the country to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers and “defame” the state of Israel. As that announcement was made, dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside Szor’s parents’ home.

Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene, where one protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished.

Abraham and Szor, speaking on Thursday, said: “We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israelis to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible.

“The threats from the Israeli government to revoke our citizenship and the death threats do not change that and will not stop the film. We thank our colleagues for the solidarity and look forward to sharing NAZA all over the world very soon.”

Support has come from 43 local human rights organisations, which last week issued a joint statement urging Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.

More than 1,500 Israeli film-makers have also put their names to a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.

Leading film-makers around the world, including Ken Loach, Joshua Oppenheimer, Paul Laverty, Laura Poitras, Nan Goldin, Richard Eyre and Hanif Kureishi, have echoed their sentiments. Oppenheimer, the US director of Oscar-nominated documentaries The Act of Killing and The Look of Silence, said, “The Israeli government is waging a full-scale intimidation campaign against film directors. I am appalled and enraged.”

/music/2026/sep/24/pete-byrne-frontman-o.headline: Pete Byrne, Naked Eyes frontman who took British new wave into the US Top 10, dies aged 74
/music/2026/sep/24/pete-byrne-frontman-o.bodyHtml:
Pete Byrne, who as frontman of the British new wave group Naked Eyes carried them to repeated chart successes in the US, has died aged 74.

Byrne died peacefully in Los Angeles on 14 September after a brief illness, the band’s website and social media announced on Wednesday.

Byrne was among the acts of the “second British invasion”, when synthpop and new wave bands from the UK, powered in part by the rise of MTV, swept into the US alongside peers including Duran Duran, A Flock of Seagulls and more.

Naked Eyes was the group he formed in the late 1970s after the failure of his groups Studio and Neon – Neon featuring future Tears for Fears members Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal as well as his future Naked Eyes bandmate Rob Fisher and others. “Rob and I found that running a band was not as interesting as writing and recording,” Byrne said. “We decided to go back to square one.”

As a duo under the new name, they signed to EMI, and their debut single became their biggest hit: a cover of the Burt Bacharach-penned Always Something There to Remind Me, powered by Byrne’s earnest boyish croon, which reached the Top 10 in the US, Canada and Australia.

Naked Eyes went on to three more Top 40 hits in the US – Promises, Promises (which reached No 11 and featured Madonna on unreleased remixes), When the Lights Go Out and (What) In the Name of Love (which was remixed by Arthur Baker) – though they never hit the Top 40 in their native UK.

The duo split after their second album, 1984’s Fuel for the Fire, having been unable to replicate their synth-heavy studio setup on tour. Byrne later put the split down to him and Fisher living in Los Angeles and London respectively, and to EMI losing faith in the project.

Byrne stepped back, writing and producing with other artists – later including a song for Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen – and recorded backing vocals for Stevie Wonder’s 1985 US No 1 Part-Time Lover. He released a solo album, The Real Illusion, in 2001, and began working with Fisher again, rebooting Naked Eyes as a solo project after Fisher’s death in 1999. Under that name Byrne released two further albums and became a familiar face on 80s revue tours, alongside the likes of the Go-Go’s and the Human League.

Music, Byrne said in 2017, has been “the main focus of my life since I was 18. Nothing has changed really. I still get up in the morning, make coffee, fiddle around on the guitar and scribble down some nonsense. And I eventually look back and say: ‘There might be something there.’”

He is survived by three children, Merlin, Dylan and Chloe, from his marriage to ex-wife Elena, and by his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve.

/us-news/2026/sep/23/trump-xi-jinping-ch.headline: US and China extend trade truce as Trump greets Xi Jinping on the tarmac to open state visit
/us-news/2026/sep/23/trump-xi-jinping-ch.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US at the start of the Chinese leader’s state visit to Washington, taking the unusual step of greeting him in person on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on the day the two countries agreed to extend their trade truce.

A lavish arrival ceremony met Xi’s plane, with a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries.

Trump and the first lady, Melania, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday evening – a departure from the usual practice of US presidents welcoming foreign leaders at the White House.

Xi’s visit coincides with world leaders gathering in New York for the United Nations general assembly, although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012.

Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters: “It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” he said. “I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

The US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan agreement – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies – Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced.

The agreement will now run until 10 January, two months beyond the date it was due to expire, Bessent told Fox News after meeting the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday.

The pageantry continues with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.

Over the two-day visit Trump and Xi will take up the simmering trade war alongside many other thorny issues, including the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability.

The White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday.

The carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony had one discordant note: Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed that while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men.

The moment was captured on a White House livestream and widely mocked online, though it was not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony released by Trump’s aides later.

The US and China have long competed to develop increasingly powerful technology, and the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially since several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, promoting instead more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

Leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically, the president and members of the administration have insisted – further raising the stakes for the US and China.

Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

Robert Mackey contributed reporting
